newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina's Fernandez challenges Congress on jobs.
newsitem.headline: Argentina's Fernandez challenges Congress on jobs.

text.p: Economy Minister Roque Fernandez challenged Congress Wednesday to take responsibility for fighting Argentina's high unemployment through a complete overhaul of labor laws, rather than a watered-down reform.

With the Peronist government and trade unions brandishing an "Act of Agreement" at businessmen who want more radical reforms, and threatening to push them through Congress, the minister reminded Congress of its "enormous responsibility".
He said that without any labor reform, unemployment would fall from its current 17.3 percent to 14 percent by the year 2000, and poverty levels to 17 percent.
With "half-hearted" reforms, he said unemployment would fall to 10 percent and poverty to 14 percent by 2000.

But, "if we eliminate all distortions we will generate 1.8 million new jobs and by the year 2000 unemployment will fall to six percent and poverty to 10 percent," he said in a speech prepared for delivery to a Buenos Aires banking conference.

"This challenge, this enormous responsibility, is in the hands of Congress and I'm sure Congress won't make mistakes, for where there is rigidity and regulations, there will be want," he said in the speech, which was obtained by Reuters.

Peronist President Carlos Menem met business and union bosses Monday to try to seek consensus on labour reform, which are one of the conditions agreed with the International Monetary Fund for debt facilities this year.
Menem has also portrayed them as the key to bringing down unemployment, which is likely to be the hottest issue in the run-up to mid-term elections in Congress in October.

But business leaders say the watered-down reforms of the "Act of Agreement" are "no use at all" because they back down on Menem's original plans to reduce employment costs by making the labor laws inherited from Juan Peron, the populist leader of the 1940s and '50s, more flexible.

The two-way agreement backs down on plans to decentralize talks on wages and working conditions, as well as proposals to swap redundancy payouts for unemployment insurance and to make union-controlled healthcare compete in a free market.
